state.claim: The recently deceased US Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg was known for her gruelling fitness regime.

candidates.quote: Have you ever wondered what keeps Supreme Court Justice and octogenarian Ruth Bader Ginsburg so sprightly? She owes it in part to the twice-weekly workouts she does with her personal trainer, Bryant Johnson, someone she’s called “the most important person” in her life. Justice Ginsburg began training with Johnson in 1999, at the urging of her late husband, after she was treated for colon cancer.

The RBG Workout: How She Stays Strong . . . and You Can Too! walks you through how to do Justice Ginsburg’s workout—from planks to squats to (full) pushups—in the comfort of your home. Each exercise is demonstrated with full-color illustrations of the Justice in workout gear and also includes tips from the bench and sidebars with Johnson’s wisdom on getting fit and staying healthy. Johnson presents the workout exactly as he does it with Justice Ginsburg, along with some variations to accommodate skill level, personal preferences, and the equipment available.

passages.P3: # In Memoriam: Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg (1933-2020)
passages.P7: President Barack Obama visits with Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg and newly confirmed Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan in the Blue Room of the White House, prior to Kagan's confirmation reception in the East Room, August 6, 2010.
passages.P9: WASHINGTON, September 21, 2020—Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States Ruth Bader Ginsburg died on September 18, after a lengthy legal career as a champion of women’s rights and gender equality.
passages.P10: Ginsburg rose to prominence as a lawyer who argued—and won—gender discrimination cases before the Supreme Court. President Bill Clinton appointed her an associate justice in 1993, making Ginsburg the second woman to serve on the nation’s highest court after Sandra Day O’Connor. (Read a brief tribute from the William J. Clinton Presidential Library.)
passages.P11: “A system of justice will be the richer for diversity of background and experience,” Ginsburg said at her swearing-in ceremony. “It will be poorer, in terms of appreciating what is at stake and the impact of its judgments, if all of its members are cast from the same mold.”
passages.P12: Weeks later, Ginsburg visited the National Archives and Records Administration. Then-Acting Archivist of the United States Trudy Peterson wanted her to see one document in particular from the agency’s holdings: the 19th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, which granted women the right to vote.
passages.P13: This year, which marks the 100th anniversary of the 19th Amendment, many Americans are mourning the passing of a lifelong defender of gender equality whom Chief Justice John Roberts called "a tireless and resolute champion of justice."
passages.P14: Ginsburg died following a recurrence of pancreatic cancer, the day after Constitution Day and hours before the start of Rosh Hashanah.

passages.P17: Notorious RBG at the National Archives
passages.P18: Letter from Ruth Bader Ginsburg Supporting the Equal Rights Amendment, April 15, 1971, DocsTeach
passages.P19: “Fight for the things you care about, but do it in a way that will lead others to join you.” National Archives Tumblr
